title: Criminal Law Basics
summary: Learn the principles of criminal law: its purposes and sources, the elements of a crime, defences such as self-defence and necessity, parties, attempts and common offences, criminal procedure and fair trial rights, and sentencing and the wider justice system. General principles only; check your own country's law.
audience: Students, paralegals, police and community workers, journalists and citizens

body.p: Criminal law defines conduct that society treats as so harmful that the state prosecutes and punishes it: theft, assault, murder, fraud, corruption, sexual offences and many more. It differs from civil law, in which private parties sue each other for remedies such as compensation, for example in contract or family disputes.

list: Retribution: punishment that the offender deserves.
Deterrence: discouraging the offender and others from offending.
Incapacitation: protecting society, for example by imprisonment.
Rehabilitation: helping offenders change and return to society.
Restorative justice: repairing harm to victims and communities, an approach close to many African traditions of reconciliation.

body.p: Crimes are defined in penal or criminal codes (common in East and West Africa and civil-law countries), in statutes, and in some countries partly by common law developed by the courts, as in South Africa. Customary law is generally not used to create crimes, because people must be able to know in advance what is criminal.

body.tip: The principle of legality, no crime and no punishment without law, means you cannot be convicted for conduct that was not a crime when you did it.

body.p: To convict someone, the prosecution must normally prove both the conduct and the mental element of the offence.

list: A voluntary act, such as taking property or striking someone.
Sometimes an omission, where there is a legal duty to act, such as a parent failing to feed a child.
Circumstances defined by the offence, such as the property belonging to another.
A result, for crimes like murder, and causation: the conduct must have caused the result.
Intention: the accused meant to do the act or bring about the result, or foresaw it as a possibility and went ahead (sometimes called dolus eventualis).
Negligence: failing to act as a reasonable person would; enough for some crimes, such as culpable homicide or causing death by negligent driving.
Strict liability offences, such as many regulatory and traffic offences, need little or no proof of fault.

body.tip: When analysing a scenario, check each element in turn: act, circumstances, result, causation and fault.

body.p: Even if the elements are present, the accused may have a defence that excludes unlawfulness or blame.

list: Private defence (self-defence): using reasonable force to repel an unlawful attack on yourself or others. The force must be necessary and proportionate to the threat.
Necessity: acting to avoid a greater harm in an emergency not caused by the accused.
Duress: being forced to commit a crime by threats of serious harm (generally not accepted for murder in many systems).

Mental illness: a person who, because of mental illness, could not understand or control their conduct is not criminally responsible, and is usually dealt with through treatment instead of punishment.
Age: children below a minimum age of criminal responsibility cannot be convicted; ages vary between countries.
Mistake of fact: an honest mistake can exclude intention.

body.p: Intoxication is generally not a full defence, and voluntary intoxication is treated strictly in most systems.

body.tip: Self-defence is judged on the facts: retaliation after the attack is over is not defence but revenge.

list: Perpetrators commit the crime, alone or together (co-perpetrators acting with a common purpose).
Accomplices help or encourage the crime and can also be convicted.
Accessories after the fact help offenders escape justice.

body.p: Attempt (going beyond preparation towards committing a crime), conspiracy (agreeing to commit a crime) and incitement (encouraging others to commit one) are crimes even if the main crime never happens.

list: Crimes against the person: murder, culpable homicide or manslaughter, assault, sexual offences, kidnapping.
Property crimes: theft, robbery (theft with violence), burglary or housebreaking, malicious damage.
Economic crimes: fraud, forgery, corruption, money laundering, cybercrime.
Crimes against the state and public order.

body.tip: Robbery is more serious than theft because it involves violence or threats; check the exact definitions in your country's code.

lessons.title: Criminal procedure and the rights of the accused

steps: Investigation: police gather evidence, interview witnesses and may search with a warrant or on legally permitted grounds.
Arrest: the person must be told the reason, informed of the right to remain silent and to a lawyer, and brought before a court within a set time, often 48 hours.
Bail: the court decides whether the accused may be released while awaiting trial, considering flight risk, danger and interference with witnesses.
Charge and trial: the prosecution presents evidence; the defence can cross-examine and present its own case.
Verdict: guilt must be proved beyond reasonable doubt.
Sentencing, followed by the possibility of appeal or review.

body.p: The accused is presumed innocent, has the right to be tried without unreasonable delay, to understand the charges (with an interpreter if needed), to legal representation, and in many countries to state-funded legal aid in serious cases. Evidence obtained through torture must be excluded.

body.tip: Long pre-trial detention is a serious problem in many African prisons; legal aid and paralegal services help people get bail hearings.

lessons.title: Sentencing and the wider justice system

body.p: Sentences include fines, community service, suspended sentences, correctional supervision, imprisonment and, in a few countries, the death penalty, which many African states have abolished in law or practice. Courts consider the seriousness of the offence, the offender's circumstances and the interests of society and victims.

list: Victims have rights to information, protection and, in many systems, compensation orders.
Diversion programmes deal with minor offences and child offenders outside the formal court process.
Child justice laws require separate procedures and detention only as a last resort.
Traditional and community justice mechanisms resolve many minor disputes, but must respect constitutional rights.

body.p: The criminal justice system employs prosecutors, defence lawyers, magistrates and judges, police and investigators, forensic specialists, correctional officers, probation officers, social workers and paralegals.

body.tip: If you are ever arrested, stay calm, ask why, say you wish to speak to a lawyer, and do not resist even if you believe the arrest is unfair.

quiz.q: Criminal law differs from civil law because:

options: No crime without a law in force at the time
The mental element, such as intention

quiz.q: An omission is criminal mainly when:
options: There is a legal duty to act

quiz.q: A person who could not understand their conduct because of mental illness is usually:
Agreeing with others to commit a crime is:
Theft with violence or threats is:
The standard of proof for a criminal conviction is:
An arrested person must usually be brought before a court within about:

options: Flight risk, danger and interference with witnesses
Deal with minor offences outside the formal court process
